progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: Stage 5 Mathematics (Pythagoras; tan and tan⁻¹ in right triangles; scale drawing); v01 (magnitude, scalar, vector; displacement, velocity, acceleration as vectors; an arrow's length shows magnitude and its head shows direction).
progression.startsWith: Last time, four metres and three metres made five. Here's why that matters. This boat points straight across a river and motors at three metres per second. But the water's moving too. Watch where it actually goes. It lands well downstream, travelling along a slant. So where does it really go, and how fast? A diagram can answer that, and today we'll see why it works.
progression.stopsAfter: scaled arrows for all three vector quantities; tip-to-tail addition with its cause; perpendicular resultants by measurement and calculation; same-line cases; subtraction by flipping, used for a change in velocity and the direction of the average acceleration. No components, sign conventions, multi-leg problems or relative velocity.
progression.nextLesson: v03, components: the same vector described by two perpendicular parts.

teaching.task: *A boat points straight across a river at 3.0 m s⁻¹, but the current carries it downstream. Where does it actually go, and how fast? And how does a diagram show a resultant, or a difference?*
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a scaled arrow carries magnitude and direction for any vector quantity (2); (2) consecutive displacements chain, so arrows join tip to tail; the resultant joins first tail to last tip (3); (3) simultaneous velocities each produce a displacement every second, so they chain the same way (4); (4) perpendicular chains make a right triangle: Pythagoras and tan⁻¹ (5); (5) on one line, sizes add or subtract (6); (6) a change is what you add to get from the first to the second, so subtracting means flipping and adding; the change can be larger than either (7, 8); (7) the average acceleration points along the change (8); (8) memory aid (9).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Last time, four metres and three metres made five. First, a vector diagram needs a scale. Now, why do we join vectors tip to tail? Think about displacements. Velocities add tip to tail too, and the river shows why.
teaching.openingDecision: opens on v01's handoff frame: the 4 m east and 3 m north arrows floating unjoined with "?". On the first sentence the 3 m arrow slides tip to tail onto the 4 m arrow and the navy 5 m resultant draws (a two-second recall; no labels change). Clear change to a plan view of a coded river: two banks running left to right, blue-grey water with faint flow lines drifting right, compass; the top-view boat plate (phys-y11-boat-top-v1.png) at the bottom bank, bow pointing north. On "second" an orange tag at the bow "heading: 3.0 m s⁻¹ across". On "goes" the boat crosses with the bow still pointing north while the flow carries it right: an amber trail draws a slant from the start pin to a landing point well downstream; a dashed grey line shows where it was aimed (straight across). On "diagram" the heading writes on: "Vector diagrams: resultant and difference", and a chip "where, and how fast?" moves to the top right.
teaching.understandingCheck: Now subtraction. This car turns a corner at a steady twenty metres per second. Before, its velocity points east. After, it points north. Its speed hasn't changed. So is its change in velocity zero, less than twenty, or more than twenty? Have a think. Your turn. A small boat heads north at two point four metres per second across a river that flows east at zero point seven zero metres per second. Using a vector diagram, find the magnitude and direction of the boat's resultant velocity. Pause here to answer. Last one. A tennis ball rolls east at three point zero metres per second, hits a wall, and rolls back west at two point zero metres per second. Using a vector diagram, find the ball's change in velocity. Pause here to answer.
